Package io.thymekit

Class Tree

java.lang.Object
io.thymekit.Tree
public final class Tree extends Object
A page is a tree of elements, and this is what can be learned by walking it.

Its own class for the reason Outline and Anchors are theirs: a question about a whole page is not a property of an element, and an element that answers one has been taught something it has no business knowing. The traversal lived on the currency for a while, which is how the outline came to live there too before it moved out; a third tenant made the pattern impossible to keep calling an exception.

Written once because it is the kind of code that goes subtly wrong in a copy: a walk that misses a branch finds nothing there and says nothing about it, which is the quietest way for a check to stop checking. Public for the reason the guards are — a check of your own over a page of yours is written the way the kit writes its own, and Outline and Anchors are the two worked examples.

  • Method Details

    • walk

      public static void walk(Object node, Predicate<Map<?,?>> visit)
      Every descriptor of a tree, whatever the tree is made of: elements, the maps they are, and collections of either, at any depth. The visitor is handed each descriptor and answers whether to go deeper into it — an illustration is a place one walker stops and another does not.

      What is handed over is required, both of it: a walk over nothing finds nothing and says so to nobody, and a check written over that passes while checking nothing. A hole inside a tree is a different matter and is walked past — a page is entitled to carry a list with a gap in it, and refusing to walk one would be this class deciding what a page may be made of. 

      
 Tree.walk(page, descriptor -> {
     if (myKit.isPicture(descriptor) && descriptor.get("alt") == null) {
         throw new MisuseException("myKit.picture", "nothing said about it");
     }
     return true;
 });
